results.description: The proximal operator of R is defined as prox_{γR}(x) = (x̄, …, x̄) where x̄ = (1/n) ∑_{i=1}^n x_i (see Section 2.1).

results.note: The proximal operator is applied to the shifted candidates rather than x directly (as expected from the ProxSkip algorithm structure), but the mean-then-broadcast operation correctly implements the proximal operator of R.

results.description: Algorithm 2: Server flips a coin θ_t, θ_t = 1 w.p. p, otherwise 0, and sends θ_t to all workers (line 2).

results.description: Algorithm 2: If θ_t = 1, worker computes x'_{i,t+1} = x̃_{i,t+1} - (γ/p) h_{i,t}, sends to server; server computes x_{i,t+1} = (1/n) ∑_{i=1}^n x'_{i,t+1} and sends back; else x_{i,t+1} = x̃_{i,t+1} (lines 6-9).

results.description: Algorithm 4: Set w_{i,0} = x_{i,0} for every worker i (line 1).
results.evidence: In proxskip_vip/algorithms.py, the function `proxskip_l_svrgda_fl` (labeled "ProxSkip-L-SVRGDA-FL (Algorithm 4)" in its docstring) initializes at lines ~117-119: `x_clients = np.repeat(x0[None, :], clients, axis=0)` (sets x_{i,0} = x0 for all workers), then immediately `snapshots = x_clients.copy()` — setting the snapshot variable w_{i,0} = x_{i,0} for every worker i. The `snapshots` array is the code's representation of the paper's w variables (used in the SVRG-style gradient estimator inside the loop).
results.note: The paper uses w_{i,0} for the snapshot/anchor variable; the code calls it `snapshots`. The initialization `snapshots = x_clients.copy()` directly implements w_{i,0} = x_{i,0}.

results.description: Algorithm 4: If ζ_t = 1, then g_{i,t} = F_{i,j_t}(x_{i,t}) - F_{i,j_t}(w_{i,t}) + F_i(w_{i,t}), where j_t ∼ Unif([m_i]) (line 5).
results.evidence:
In proxskip_vip/algorithms.py, function `proxskip_l_svrgda_fl` (Algorithm 4), the gradient for each client is computed as:
  g = operator(x_clients[i], i, sample) - operator(snapshots[i], i, sample) + operator(snapshots[i], i, None)
which exactly matches F_{i,j_t}(x_{i,t}) - F_{i,j_t}(w_{i,t}) + F_i(w_{i,t}).
The sample index j_t is drawn uniformly via `sample = int(rng.integers(samples[i]))`, i.e., j_t ~ Unif([m_i]). The snapshot variable `snapshots[i]` acts as w_{i,t}. The `operator(..., None)` call (no sample index) returns the full gradient F_i(w_{i,t}).
results.note: The code applies this SVRG formula unconditionally on every step (not conditioned on ζ_t=1), but this is consistent with Algorithm 4 where the SVRG gradient is always used — the ζ_t=1 event in the paper corresponds to a snapshot refresh (`snapshots = x_clients.copy()` when `refresh` is True), not a switch in gradient formula.

results.description: Algorithm 4: Update w_{i,t+1} = x_{i,t} if ζ_t = 1, otherwise w_{i,t} (line 6).
results.evidence: In proxskip_vip/algorithms.py, the function `proxskip_l_svrgda_fl` (Algorithm 4) implements the snapshot update. `snapshots` represents w_{i,t}, `refresh` is the Bernoulli variable ζ_t (`refresh = rng.random() < snapshot_probability`), and `x_clients` is x_{i,t}. The update at lines ~148-149: `if refresh: snapshots = x_clients.copy()` — when ζ_t=1, w_{i,t+1} = x_{i,t}; when ζ_t=0, snapshots remains unchanged (w_{i,t+1} = w_{i,t}).
results.note: The update is applied before incrementing `local_steps`, and uses `x_clients` (the current iterate before the communication step), matching the paper's line 6 in Algorithm 4.

results.description: Algorithm 4: x̃_{i,t+1} = x_{i,t} - γ (g_{i,t} - h_{i,t}) (line 7).
results.evidence: proxskip_vip/algorithms.py, function `proxskip_l_svrgda_fl` (Algorithm 4), line: `xhat[i] = x_clients[i] - gamma * (g - h[i])`. Here `xhat[i]` = x̃_{i,t+1}, `x_clients[i]` = x_{i,t}, `g` is the SVRG gradient estimator g_{i,t}, and `h[i]` = h_{i,t}. This exactly implements x̃_{i,t+1} = x_{i,t} - γ(g_{i,t} - h_{i,t}).
results.note: The gradient `g` is computed as the SVRG estimator: operator(x_clients[i], i, sample) - operator(snapshots[i], i, sample) + operator(snapshots[i], i, None), which is the full g_{i,t} from Algorithm 4.

results.description: Algorithm 4: If θ_t = 1, worker computes x'_{i,t+1} = x̃_{i,t+1} - (γ/p) h_{i,t}, sends to server; server computes x_{i,t+1} = (1/n) ∑_{i=1}^n x'_{i,t+1} and sends back; else x_{i,t+1} = x̃_{i,t+1} (lines 8-12).
results.evidence: In proxskip_vip/algorithms.py, the function `proxskip_l_svrgda_fl` (labeled "ProxSkip-L-SVRGDA-FL (Algorithm 4)") implements lines 8-12: (1) `xhat[i] = x_clients[i] - gamma * (g - h[i])` computes x̃_{i,t+1}; (2) When θ_t=1 (communication event fires): `candidates = xhat - (gamma / communication_probability) * h` computes x'_{i,t+1} = x̃_{i,t+1} - (γ/p)h_{i,t} for all workers; `x_new = np.mean(candidates, axis=0)` computes server average (1/n)∑x'_{i,t+1}; `x_clients[:] = x_new` distributes result back to all clients; (3) When θ_t=0 (else branch): `x_clients = xhat` sets x_{i,t+1} = x̃_{i,t+1}. results.description: Algorithm 4: h_{i,t+1} = h_{i,t} + (γ/p)(x_{i,t+1} - x̃_{i,t+1}) (line 14).
results.evidence: In proxskip_vip/algorithms.py, the `proxskip_l_svrgda_fl` function (Algorithm 4) updates h at line ~163: `h += (communication_probability / gamma) * (x_new[None, :] - xhat)`. This computes h_{i,t+1} = h_{i,t} + (p/γ)(x_new - xhat), using factor (p/γ). The rubric claims line 14 should be h_{i,t+1} = h_{i,t} + (γ/p)(x_{i,t+1} - x̃_{i,t+1}), requiring factor (γ/p). The code uses the inverse coefficient (p/γ) rather than (γ/p), so the specific formula in the rubric is NOT implemented.
results.note: Note that the same (p/γ) pattern appears in Algorithm 2 (proxskip_fl). It is possible the paper uses a different convention or the code is implementing an equivalent rearrangement. However, taking the claim at face value — that line 14 uses (γ/p) — the code contradicts this with (p/γ).

results.description: In the deterministic case (ProxSkip-GDA), the estimator g_t is the exact operator F(x_t) (see Section 3.2, deterministic case).
results.evidence: In proxskip_vip/algorithms.py, the `proxskip_fl` function (lines 49-101) implements ProxSkip-GDA. At line 83, indices are computed as: `indices = [int(rng.integers(samples[i])) if stochastic and samples else None for i in range(clients)]`. In the deterministic case (`stochastic=False`), `indices[i]` is always `None`. At line 86, `g = operator(x_clients[i], i, indices[i])` thus calls `operator(x_clients[i], i, None)`, which by convention (also confirmed in `proxskip_l_svrgda_fl` at line 143 where `None` means full operator) is the exact operator F(x_t). The update at line 87 then uses this as `xhat[i] = x_clients[i] - gamma * (g - h[i])`, matching ProxSkip-GDA with g_t = F(x_t).
results.note: The `None` index signals the full/exact operator evaluation, as confirmed by its use in `proxskip_l_svrgda_fl` at line 143 where `operator(snapshots[i], i, None)` is the full-batch snapshot gradient. The deterministic path in `proxskip_fl` indeed uses the exact operator.

results.description: Eigenvalues of matrices B_{ij} lie in [0, 1].

results.description: Vectors a_{ij} and c_{ij} are generated from N_d(0, I_d) distribution.
results.evidence: In proxskip_vip/games.py, the QuadraticGame.__init__ generates 'a' and 'c' via `_psd_matrix(rng, dimension, eigenvalue_min, eigenvalue_max)`, which performs QR decomposition on a random normal matrix and constructs a PSD matrix with controlled eigenvalues (between eigenvalue_min=0.01 and eigenvalue_max=1.0). This is NOT sampling from N_d(0, I_d). The offsets are generated as `rng.normal(size=2*dimension)` (standard normal vectors), but those are the bias/offset terms, not a_{ij} and c_{ij}. No code in the repository generates a_{ij} or c_{ij} as vectors from N_d(0, I_d).
results.note: The paper's Section 5 likely defines a_{ij} and c_{ij} as vectors used to construct the quadratic payoffs, but the code implements them as PSD matrices built from QR decomposition. The generation mechanism differs fundamentally from N_d(0,I_d) sampling.

results.description: The data is heterogeneous: A_{ij}, B_{ij}, C_{ij}, a_{ij}, c_{ij} are different across clients.
results.evidence: In proxskip_vip/games.py, QuadraticGame.__init__ iterates over all (client, sample) pairs and independently draws a=_psd_matrix(rng,...), c=_psd_matrix(rng,...), b=_psd_matrix(rng,...), and offsets=rng.normal(...) for each pair using a sequential RNG. results.description: The problem is a constrained matrix game: min_{x∈Δ} max_{y∈Δ} f(x,y) = (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^n x^⊤ A_i y, where Δ is the (d-1)-dimensional standard simplex.
results.evidence: proxskip_vip/games.py: The `MatrixGame` class implements a constrained matrix game where: (1) `matrices[client, i, j] = weights[client, i] * (1 - exp(-0.8*|i-j|))` creates per-client matrices A_i; (2) `global_matrix = matrices.mean(axis=0)` computes (1/n)Σ A_i; (3) operator returns `np.concatenate((a @ x[self.row:], -a.T @ x[:self.row]))` which is the gradient of x^T A y wrt (x,y) giving the min/max directions; (4) `project()` calls `project_simplex` on both x and y components, constraining both to the standard simplex Δ; (5) `dual_gap()` computes `max_y x1^T A y - min_x A x2` consistent with the saddle-point formulation. The experiment in `experiments.py` is labeled "Policemen-Burglar matrix game, Appendix H.5" and uses `game.dual_gap` as the metric.
results.note: The number of clients n corresponds to the finite-sum index; the operator used in the experiment is the per-client operator (one sample per client), meaning the finite sum is over clients. The simplex dimension is (row-1)-dimensional and (col-1)-dimensional respectively.

results.description: The performance metric is the duality gap, defined as max_{y∈Δ} f(x̂, y) - min_{x∈Δ} f(x, ŷ) at (x̂, ŷ).
results.evidence: proxskip_vip/games.py lines 253-258: MatrixGame.dual_gap(x) computes max_player = np.max(x1 @ a) (i.e., max_{y∈Δ} f(x̂, y)) and min_player = np.min(a @ x2) (i.e., min_{x∈Δ} f(x, ŷ)), returning max_player - min_player. The class is explicitly labeled "Constrained Policemen-Burglar matrix game (Appendix H.5)". In proxskip_vip/experiments.py, run_matrix() (line 174-201) uses game.dual_gap as the metric (lines 188, 195) and returns ylabel="Duality gap" (line 201).
results.note: The iterates are time-averaged (running/count) before being passed to dual_gap for ProxSkip-GDA-FL and Local GDA, while Local EG uses dual_gap directly. The formula itself matches the rubric exactly.

results.description: The duality gap is evaluated on the moving average of the iterates: (1/(K+1)) Σ_{k=0}^K x_k, where x_k is the output after k communication rounds.
results.evidence: In proxskip_vip/experiments.py, the `run_matrix` function (Policemen-Burglar experiment, Appendix H.5) defines a `moving_metric()` closure that accumulates a running sum of iterates and evaluates the duality gap on `running / count`. Concretely: `running = running + np.asarray(x); count += 1; return game.dual_gap(running / count)`. This is applied to ProxSkip-GDA-FL and Local GDA methods (Local EG uses the raw dual_gap directly). The pattern matches (1/(K+1)) Σ_{k=0}^K x_k exactly.
results.note: The moving average metric is used for ProxSkip-GDA-FL and Local GDA, but Local EG uses `game.dual_gap` directly (not the moving average). The rubric says "all" methods, but the primary claim about evaluating duality gap on the moving average is clearly implemented for the main methods in the Policemen-Burglar experiment.
